The paper proposes a multilayered plasmonic shell cloak to reduce scattering at multiple optical frequencies simultaneously.
The cloak exploits the frequency dispersion and negative polarizability of plasmonic materials.
A two-layered cloak design is demonstrated for a dielectric sphere of permittivity 3 and diameter 200 nm.
The cloak targets free-space wavelengths of 500 nm and 625 nm for scattering reduction.
Shell thicknesses are approximately 107.5 nm for the inner shell and 131.5 nm for the outer shell.
Scattering efficiency is reduced by about 30-fold at 500 nm and 120-fold at 625 nm compared to the uncloaked particle.
The cloak maintains significant performance even with realistic Ohmic losses in the plasmonic materials.
The cloaking effect is polarization independent and works for both TM and TE polarizations.
The approach uses an extension of Mie theory for multilayered spheres to calculate scattering coefficients.
Numerical simulations using finite-integration technique software validate the analytical results.
The cloaking effect restores uniform electric field amplitude and planar phase fronts in the near field.
A sharp scattering peak appears near 580 nm due to dipolar and quadrupolar plasmonic resonances but is suppressed by losses.
The method is nonresonant and thus offers broader bandwidth than transformation optics cloaks.
Adding more plasmonic layers can extend cloaking to more frequencies without significantly increasing size.
The cloak layers add only a few percent thickness relative to the object size, avoiding bulky designs.
The technique can be extended to lower frequencies using metamaterial plasmonic covers.
Near-field cloaking allows potential application to collections of nanoparticles larger than the wavelength.
The cloak cancels dominant electric dipole scattering but also reduces higher-order multipoles.
The design assumes Drude-type dispersive plasmonic materials with plasma frequencies near the target wavelengths.
The research demonstrates feasibility with current nanotechnology for fabricating multilayered nanoshells.
